title: You almost skipped her.
paragraphs: You almost skipped her.

Not because her story wasn’t important…
but because it was too uncomfortable to sit with.
Her name is Tamar.
And what happened to her should disturb you.
Because it still happens—just quieter.

She wasn’t reckless.
She wasn’t flirting with danger.
She was obeying.

Her brother Amnon pretended to be sick.
Their father, King David, sent her to care for him.
That’s where it began.

A closed room.
A false need.
A setup disguised as family concern.
And somewhere deep inside, something felt off.
But she went anyway.

Because authority said go.
Because love doesn’t suspect betrayal.
Because sometimes evil doesn’t look like evil until it’s too late.
Then it happened.
The moment where everything shifted from normal to irreversible.
He grabbed her.
She resisted.
She pleaded.
“Don’t do this, my brother… such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing.” (2 Samuel 13:12)
Read that again.
She named it clearly.

Sin.
Disgrace.
Wrong.
But he didn’t listen.
“He refused to listen to her… and being stronger, he violated her.” (2 Samuel 13:14)

Strength used to destroy.
Authority twisted into violence.
Desire turned into sin without restraint.
And God saw it.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The story doesn’t end with the act.
It gets worse.

After he took what he wanted,
he hated her.
“Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred… greater than the love with which he had loved her.” (2 Samuel 13:15)
That’s sin.

It promises connection,
then leaves disgust.

It whispers desire,
then produces hatred.
You’ve seen that pattern before.

Maybe not this extreme…
but the same root.
Take. Use. Discard.
And then pretend nothing happened.
He sent her away.

Not just rejected…
erased.

She tore her robe.
Put ashes on her head.
Walked away crying.

Public shame.
Private devastation.
And then silence.
Her brother Absalom told her to keep quiet.
Her father heard about it…
…and did nothing.
Nothing.
Let that sit.

The king.
The protector.
The father.
Did nothing.
You know that kind of silence.

When something wrong happens…
and nobody speaks.

When truth is buried to keep peace.
When justice is delayed until it dies.
When pain is ignored because it’s inconvenient.
God saw it.
“Tamar lived in her brother Absalom’s house, a desolate woman.” (2 Samuel 13:20)
Desolate.
Not just hurt.
Not just grieving.

Empty.
Isolated.
Forgotten.
A life paused in trauma… while everyone else moved on.
And maybe that’s where this hits you.
Because your story has silence in it too.

Something happened.
Someone crossed a line.
Someone took what wasn’t theirs—respect, trust, innocence.
And nobody stepped in.
Nobody fixed it.
Nobody even acknowledged it properly.
You carried it.
You buried it.
You learned to function around it.
But you never healed from it.
God saw it.
You knew.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Tamar’s story isn’t just about what was done to her.
It’s about the brokenness of a world where sin goes unchecked.

Amnon’s lust.
David’s passivity.
Absalom’s delayed revenge.
All of it points to something deeper:
Humanity cannot fix itself.

Even kings fail.
Even families collapse.
Even justice systems break.
So where does that leave you?
Right here.
At the edge of something uncomfortable but necessary:
You don’t just live in a broken world…
You contribute to it.

Maybe not like Amnon.
But in smaller, quieter ways.

Silence when you should speak.
Compromise when you know the truth.
Selfishness dressed up as survival.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
Read that again.
All.
That’s why Tamar’s story doesn’t end in 2 Samuel.
It echoes forward…
to a cross.
Because injustice like hers demands more than sympathy.
It demands justice.
And God didn’t ignore it.
He absorbed it.
“Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows…” (Isaiah 53:4)
Jesus didn’t stand at a distance from broken stories like Tamar’s.
He stepped into them.
He took the weight of sin—every act of violence, every silence, every failure—and carried it to the cross.
“And by His wounds we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5)
Not minimized.
Not ignored.
Healed.
That’s the part you can’t skip.
Because healing doesn’t come from pretending it didn’t happen.
It comes from bringing it into the light of Christ.
Sin—whether done by you or against you—must be answered.
And at the cross, it is.
Fully.
So now you’re standing in a moment Tamar never got in her story:
A decision.

Will you stay silent…
or will you bring everything into the light?

Will you keep carrying it…
or finally surrender it to the One who sees, knows, and heals?
Because Jesus doesn’t just expose sin.
He redeems.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior

And if something in you is stirring right now… that tension, that weight, that sense that God is confronting something deeper—you don’t need another distraction. You need truth that keeps working on you, correcting you, rebuilding you.

Not surface motivation.
Transformation.
Follow, because this isn’t the end of what God is uncovering.
And if you felt that moment—that quiet recognition—don’t hide it.
Say it.

“I won’t stay silent anymore.”
or
“Jesus, I need healing.”
